views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should come to the Buenos Aires table prepared to negotiate a freeze, not to escalate or to capitulate. Going into the G20 dinner with Xi, our aim should be a truce that stalls the Jan 1 rise of List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25% and defers the threatened $267B tranche, offering limited, face-saving concessions (higher US purchases, lower our own import tariffs, market-access steps) while refusing to accept permanent tariffs or binding structural reform. Do not retaliate further against the $267B threat, and do not concede the core IP/tech-transfer demands — both would worsen our position.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high but not existential. Tariffs now cover roughly $250B of our exports to the US across Lists 1/2/3, with List 3 scheduled to jump to 25% on Jan 1 and a further $267B threatened (NYT, Politico, CNBC). The economy is already showing strain: Q3 growth of 6.5% was the slowest since 2009 (CNN), the yuan has fallen ~9% since April (CNN/SCMP), the PBoC has cut reserve requirements four times, and export fair attendees report crushed margins, factory closures, and production shifting to Vietnam (SCMP). That supports a +0.6 threat score well above the 'high' anchor. But this is not existential: reserves remain large, there is no financial crisis, and a de-escalation path exists. On action, escalation would be self-defeating given the opponent's threatened near-total tariff coverage, yet full concession (accepting permanent tariffs / structural reform) is domestically untenable and unnecessary — reports show US moderates (Mnuchin, Kudlow) are themselves pushing for a truce that delays the escalation and holds off new tariffs (NYT). That alignment of interests justifies a negotiating stance (action_score +0.15) that trades limited, face-saving concessions to freeze the escalation and buy time, rather than conceding fundamentals pre-emptively.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports covered by US tariffs; List 3 to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019, with $267B more threatened
Q3 2018 GDP growth 6.5%, slowest since 2009, deepening slowdown
Yuan down ~9% since April; PBoC cut reserve ratios four times
Chinese exporters reporting crushed margins, closures, and relocation to Vietnam
US moderates within the administration pushing for a G20 truce that delays escalation
Nov 1 Trump-Xi phone call agreed a G20 meeting — a live de-escalation avenue
China has retaliated proportionally at every step (~$110B of US goods)

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
China's economy grew 6.5% in Q3 2018, slowest since 2009, under pressure from US tariffs on more than $250B of exports.
Yuan down >9% vs USD in six months; exporters' margins crushed, many to close or move to Vietnam.
PBoC freed 750 billion yuan in a 4th reserve-requirement cut to prop up growth amid trade-war pressure.
Administration plans to raise tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods to 25% Jan 1, plus $267B more; moderates urging a truce that delays the increase.
